strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: 50 runs per condition, three algorithms, multiple reward settings, and real robotics benchmarks with proper ablations
Addresses a genuine practical gap in the literature—SO(3) action representations in RL are understudied despite importance for robotics
Deep mechanistic analysis that goes beyond empirical comparisons: investigates exploration distributions, entropy-action interactions, and Q-function learning with multi-covers
Clear, implementation-ready practical guidelines with code listings for practitioners, addressing a real pain point in robotics research
Excellent execution quality: thorough design, extensive hyperparameter tuning (100+ runs per environment), detailed appendix with ablations
Well-written and well-organized presentation of complex material, making it accessible to practitioners
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily an empirical evaluation study that confirms expected intuitions rather than introducing new algorithms, representations, or theoretical insights

Incomplete scope: restricted to state-based observations (no visual learning), small networks (64-256 units), and standard policy classes; doesn't address image-based or large-scale settings
SAC's off-manifold action handling is ad-hoc, keeping actions off-manifold during sampling while computing log-probabilities on-manifold—an inelegant solution to a fundamental incompatibility
Limited engagement with related work and alternative approaches: minimal comparison to Schuck et al. (2025) and no discussion of 6D representations commonly used in robotics
Statistical rigor could be stronger: standard deviations reported but no significance tests; some overlapping error bars claimed as clear winners

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem in robotics with comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple representations, algorithms, and benchmarks
Systematic hypothesis-driven analysis (Section 3.3) with clean experimental design isolating representation effects via idealized environment
Thorough implementation details and practical code snippets (Appendix A.3) that aid reproducibility and practitioner adoption
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (small networks, state-based observations, simulation-only) and extensive ablation studies
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily compares existing representations without introducing new methods or theoretical insights into why differences occur in RL settings

Recommendations are weak and task-dependent, undermining practical utility: RoboSuite results show small differences within error bars; Euler angles competitive in drone racing; gaps narrow in restricted-rotation tasks
Circular experimental design: αmax parameter is set such that tangent-space singularities are 'always out of reach,' artificially constraining the problem space to favor the recommended solution
Insufficient statistical rigor: no formal significance testing, only 50 runs for main results (Table 2), overlapping error bars in many comparisons yet strong claims of superiority made

Hyperparameter tuning bias: separate Bayesian optimization per representation (100 runs) without analyzing whether tuning effort/difficulty differs across representations, potentially confounding performance differences

Training-execution mismatch inadequately addressed: practical compromise of projecting mean inside network but sampling in Euclidean space creates discrepancy whose implications for convergence are glossed over

Scope limitations significantly undermine generalization claims: restricted to small networks (64-256 units), state-based observations only, simulation-only with no sim-to-real analysis; modern RL increasingly uses vision and large models
Ad-hoc solutions to identified problems: entropy regularization fix (scaling tangent actions) is workaround lacking principled justification; no comparison with manifold-aware entropy regularization
Missing key comparisons: no evaluation of manifold-specific optimization methods, limited comparison with recent work (Schuck et al. 2025), restricted to PPO/SAC/TD3 algorithms
Theoretical gaps: why quaternion double-cover harms learning or entropy interacts differently is only empirically observed without analyzing optimization landscape or gradient flow dynamics

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem with clear relevance to robotics practitioners
Comprehensive empirical methodology spanning three RL algorithms, multiple reward settings, and three robotic benchmarks with proper statistical rigor (50 seeds)
Thorough causal analysis investigating why representations differ through well-motivated hypotheses with supporting ablations
High-quality presentation with clear writing, excellent visualizations, and implementation-ready code examples that lower barriers to adoption
Novel empirical insights about exploration dynamics, entropy-manifold interactions, and why local tangent vectors outperform mathematically 'superior' representations
Extensive reproducibility details, ablation studies, and appendix materials demonstrating scientific rigor
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an empirical validation of expectations rather than introducing new algorithms, theory, or fundamental insights about SO(3) representations
Main recommendation (use local tangent vectors) is somewhat unsurprising given their known mathematical properties—the contribution is validation rather than discovery
Scope limitations: standard robotic tasks only, simulation-based without real robot validation, small networks (64-256 units), deterministic environments
Incomplete theoretical understanding: explanations remain largely intuitive rather than formal (e.g., entropy-manifold interaction in A.4 lacks formal analysis)

Hyperparameter tuning trade-offs not fully explored: different representations require different tuning strategies and tricks (e.g., custom initialization for Euler angles), making it unclear how much performance difference is due to representation vs. hyperparameter mismatch
Weak sparse reward results limit applicability: most representations struggle significantly, reducing practical relevance since findings primarily apply to dense reward settings
Missing ablations on observation representations, computational costs, and applicability to other Lie groups (SE(3), etc.); limited engagement with geometric deep learning literature
SAC compromise (project mean, sample in Euclidean space) is pragmatic but theoretically unsatisfying; no formal treatment of impact on log-probability computation

strengths: Comprehensive systematic evaluation of SO(3) representations across three major RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, TD3) with both dense and sparse rewards across multiple environments
Clear mathematical exposition of SO(3) geometry and practical explanation of why representation choice matters (singularities, discontinuities, non-uniqueness)
Mechanistic analysis going beyond performance metrics to understand how representations affect exploration, entropy regularization, and gradient dynamics
Reproducible work with released code, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and implementation snippets for practitioners
Practical guidelines and actionable recommendations for practitioners choosing rotation representations
Testing across multiple domains (idealized rotation environments, drone trajectory tracking, drone racing, robot manipulation) provides reasonable validation breadth
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily a comparative empirical study with no new representation schemes, algorithms, or theoretical frameworks introduced; contribution is incremental rather than advancing the field

Inconsistent and inconclusive results with large error bars throughout; performance differences often within noise margins; recommendations are frequently algorithm-specific and task-specific rather than universal

Unfair experimental comparisons: hyperparameters are optimized separately for each representation and environment, making it unclear whether performance differences stem from representation choice or differential tuning effort; no statistical significance testing despite large standard deviations

Limited generalization: experiments restricted to small networks (2-3 layers, 64-128 units), state-based observations, and relatively simple robotic tasks; unclear how findings transfer to visual RL, higher-dimensional action spaces, or modern RL variants

Theoretical gaps: paper identifies phenomena (e.g., entropy driving Euler angles toward singularities) but lacks principled solutions; limited theoretical framework for predicting when representations will succeed in new domains

Implementation and practical concerns: the recommended tangent space projection is pragmatic but may not optimally preserve gradient flow; requires specialized knowledge (Exp/Log maps) not all practitioners possess; SAC's entropy issues (Section A.1.3) suggest fundamental unresolved limitations

Presentation: key results scattered between main text and extensive appendix; dense notation; important findings (conflicting gradients, entropy analysis) relegated to appendix; large error bars in figures make visual assessment difficult

Experimental design issues: only 50 runs for some experiments; hyperparameter sweep methodology (100 runs per environment per representation) is computationally expensive and may artificially favor certain representations; missing ablations on network architecture effects

strengths: Comprehensive systematic empirical evaluation of SO(3) representations across three major RL algorithms and multiple robotic benchmarks with 50+ runs per condition
Clear mathematical exposition of SO(3) representations, their geometric properties (smoothness, uniqueness, singularities), and constraint-handling approaches
Extensive experimental work including ablation studies on entropy regularization, action scaling, and alternative implementations (unit-centering, 6D representations)
Practical focus directly addressing real challenges in robotic orientation control with implementation details and reproducibility resources
Well-organized presentation of representations and their mathematical properties in accessible way for practitioners unfamiliar with manifold learning
weaknesses: Severely limited novelty: This is a benchmarking study of existing representations across existing algorithms with no new methods, algorithmic innovations, or theoretical contributions—reads as technical report rather than research contribution

Core conclusions are contradictory and inconclusive: Delta representations sometimes outperform but inconsistently; SAC results acknowledged as 'not conclusive'; Euler angles work in some cases; final answer is 'it depends on algorithm and environment'

Five hypotheses in Section 3.3 are weakly validated: H1 (smooth representations converge faster) contradicted by results; connections between representation geometry and learned behavior not rigorously established; H3-H5 mostly post-hoc explanations

Insufficient statistical rigor: High standard deviations in Table 2 (e.g., ±13.4) with no significance testing; large variances suggest many differences may not be statistically significant; results appear sensitive to seeds and hyperparameter tuning

Weak practical guidance: Recommendations in Section 3.4 are vague ('prefer delta actions', 'pay special attention to sparse rewards') or obvious; no principled framework for practitioners choosing representations for new problems; practitioners could reach same conclusions through their own testing

Limited scope reducing generalization: Pure rotation environment is oversimplified; only 3 robot benchmarks (drone, manipulation); no modern visual RL or complex environments; simple MLP architectures; unclear if findings transfer beyond these specific tasks

Insufficient analysis of core phenomena: When smooth representations underperform, explanations are unsatisfying (attributed to 'multi-modal Q-functions'); interaction between representation properties and algorithm design poorly understood; why projections sometimes help/hurt is analyzed only superficially

Missing rigorous evaluation of hypotheses: H1 central intuition contradicted by inconsistent empirical results; representation-exploration connection not formally established; entropy regularization analysis reveals SAC-specific issues orthogonal to representation choice; explanations often post-hoc rather than predictive

Inadequate for top-tier venue standards: No novel methodology, algorithmic innovations, or theoretical contributions; results lack consistent statistical significance; insights are mostly obvious or contradictory; paper doesn't provide sufficient new understanding of RL on manifolds or clear guidance for practitioners

High-variance results and methodological concerns: Variable hyperparameter tuning intensity across environments (50-100 runs); unclear if all representations received equal tuning effort; no analysis of sensitivity to initialization; potential cherry-picking of results emphasizing strongest cases

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical evaluation across multiple RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, TD3), SO(3) representations, and robotic benchmarks with rigorous experimental methodology (50 runs, reported standard deviations)
Addresses a genuine practical problem in robotic RL with clear, actionable recommendations (e.g., preferring delta tangent vector representations in local frame)
Well-organized presentation with accessible main text and detailed appendices; clear figures effectively communicate findings
Five well-motivated hypotheses systematically tested with extensive ablations examining entropy regularization effects, projections, action scaling, and unit rotation centering
Evaluation spans both idealized rotation-only environments and realistic robotic benchmarks (drone control, manipulation tasks), demonstrating practical applicability
Strong foundation in differential geometry with correct mathematical treatment of SO(3) and various parameterizations
weaknesses: Limited novelty - this is fundamentally a comprehensive empirical survey of existing representations rather than introducing new methods or theoretical insights
Narrow scope: only three standard RL algorithms, focus only on continuous orientation control, no exploration of modern methods (diffusion policies, transformers), and limited set of robotic tasks
Insufficient theoretical analysis - while intuition is provided, the paper lacks formal theoretical guarantees or principled explanations for why representations matter beyond empirical observation

Incomplete experimental analysis: no formal statistical significance testing despite high variance in results; hyperparameter tuning per environment could bias results; some pathological behaviors (e.g., entropy regularization issues in Hypothesis 3) acknowledged but not deeply investigated
Presentation issues: Table 2 with numerous metrics is difficult to interpret; critical analysis relegated to appendices; some key insights buried in dense exposition
Limited discussion of generalization: unclear how findings transfer beyond rigid rotations, minimal sim-to-real implications discussion, no guidance on when insights may break down

Methodological concerns: separating hyperparameter tuning per environment while varying representations introduces potential confounds; initialization fairness across representations not fully addressed
